issues.legal_issue: Children born from a void or voidable marriage may claim rights in their parents’ property, including the parents’ interest in ancestral property, but not in the property of other persons.
material_facts: A man’s second marriage occurred while his first marriage was subsisting, and the children of the second marriage were treated as children of a void marriage.
The dispute concerned partition of property found to be ancestral property.
The children sought a share in the property of their father.
issues.conclusion: The Court expressed the view that the children could claim rights in their parents’ property, whether self-acquired or ancestral, but not in the property of anyone other than their parents. Because this view differed from earlier Supreme Court decisions, the Court referred the matter for reconsideration by a larger Bench rather than finally disposing of the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(1) and (2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, confer legitimacy on children of void or voidable marriages, and Section 16(3) limits their property rights to the property of their parents without distinguishing between self-acquired and ancestral property. The Court relied on the purposive and beneficial interpretation discussed in Parayankandiyal Eravath Kanapravan Kalliani Amma v. K. Devi, including its recognition that the legal fiction extends to succession to parents’ property. It considered Jinia Keotin v. Kumar Sitaram Manjhi, Neelamma v. Sarojamma, and Bharatha Matha v. R. Vijaya Renganathan to have adopted an unduly narrow interpretation requiring reconsideration. The Court also referred to Articles 37, 39(f), and 300A of the Constitution and the discussion of judicial application of Directive Principles in Kesavananda Bharati.

predicates.property_rights_dispute: A dispute concerns a child’s claimed rights in property.
predicates.child_from_void_or_voidable_marriage: The child was born from a marriage that is void or voidable.
predicates.parental_property_claim: The child claims property belonging to one or both parents.

issues.definition: When a property-rights dispute involves a child born from a void or voidable marriage claiming a parent’s property, the child is entitled to parental property, including ancestral property.

issues.legal_issue: A child born from a void or voidable marriage cannot claim property belonging to someone other than the child’s parents under the statutory legitimacy rule.
material_facts: The children’s claimed rights arose from their father’s second marriage, which was treated as void.
The property dispute concerned the father’s property; the Court considered whether the statutory rights could extend beyond the parents’ property.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the statutory property rights of such children are confined to the property of their parents and do not extend to the property of another person. The Court referred its differing interpretation of the statutory scheme to a larger Bench for reconsideration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(3) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, expressly preserves rights only in the property of the parents and excludes rights in the property of any other person. In Parayankandiyal Eravath Kanapravan Kalliani Amma v. K. Devi, the Court recognized that the legitimacy fiction operates for succession to the parents’ property but not to the property of other relations. The Court considered the contrary or narrower reasoning in Jinia Keotin v. Kumar Sitaram Manjhi, Neelamma v. Sarojamma, and Bharatha Matha v. R. Vijaya Renganathan and referred the matter for larger-Bench reconsideration.

predicates.property_rights_dispute: A dispute concerns a child’s claimed rights in property.
predicates.child_from_void_or_voidable_marriage: The child was born from a marriage that is void or voidable.
predicates.property_belongs_to_nonparent: The property claimed belongs to someone other than the child’s parent or parents.

issues.definition: When a child born from a void or voidable marriage claims property belonging to someone other than the parents, the child is not entitled to that property under the statutory legitimacy rule.

issues.legal_issue: A child born from a void or voidable marriage may claim only the share of joint family property that becomes the parent’s property and cannot demand partition of that property during the parent’s lifetime.
material_facts: The children sought partition of ancestral joint family property during their father’s lifetime.
The Court considered their entitlement in joint family property to be confined to the property falling to their parent’s share.
The father was alive when the partition claim was made.
issues.conclusion: The Court expressed the view that such children cannot claim partition by their own right during their parent’s lifetime and may exercise their right only after the parent’s death; their entitlement is to the property that becomes the parent’s property. The Court referred the matter to a larger Bench for reconsideration and did not finally dispose of the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, gives children of void or voidable marriages rights in their parents’ property. Applying that provision to joint family property, the Court reasoned that the child’s right is limited to the parent’s share, which becomes the parent’s absolute property upon partition, and that the child cannot demand partition while the parent is alive. The Court’s purposive approach drew on Parayankandiyal Eravath Kanapravan Kalliani Amma v. K. Devi and the constitutional values discussed under Articles 37 and 39(f); it expressed disagreement with the narrower approach in Jinia Keotin, Neelamma, and Bharatha Matha and referred the issue to a larger Bench.

rule.if: partition_dispute and child_from_void_or_voidable_marriage and joint_family_property and parent_alive

predicates.partition_dispute: A proceeding seeks partition of property.
predicates.child_from_void_or_voidable_marriage: The child was born from a marriage that is void or voidable.
predicates.joint_family_property: The property sought to be partitioned is joint family property.
predicates.parent_alive: The parent whose share is claimed is alive when partition is sought.

issues.definition: In a partition dispute involving joint family property, a child born from a void or voidable marriage cannot demand partition of the parent’s property while that parent is alive.
